1928–2012 · Germany and United States

Ulric Neisser

German-born American psychologist. His book Cognitive Psychology (1967) gave the field its name, and he later argued for studying memory and perception in real life.

Biography

Ulric Gustav Neisser was born in Kiel, Germany, in 1928. His family, of Jewish descent, emigrated to the United States in 1931. He studied at Harvard, where he became interested in information theory with George A. Miller, and at Swarthmore he met Wolfgang Köhler, from whom he took his interest in Gestalt. He taught at Brandeis, Pennsylvania, Cornell and Emory. He died in Ithaca in 2012.

Questions he investigated

  • How does the mind transform, store and retrieve information from the senses?
  • Are laboratory experiments representative of how we remember in everyday life?
  • What do intelligence scores really tell us, and why do they change over time?

Contributions

In 1967 he published Cognitive Psychology, the first textbook to bring together under one name the studies of attention, perception, memory and language that had emerged since the 1950s. He defined cognition as all the processes by which sensory input is transformed, reduced, elaborated, stored, recovered and used. The book became the founding charter of cognitive psychology.

Nine years later, in Cognition and Reality, he criticised that same field's drift towards artificial experiments and proposed the perceptual cycle: what we expect guides what we explore, and what we find corrects what we expect. He argued for ecological validity and studied memory in real situations, such as John Dean's testimony in the Watergate case or people's memories of what they were doing when the Challenger space shuttle exploded.

Collaborations, influences and disagreements

He combined very different influences: information theory, Gestalt and the ecological psychology of James and Eleanor Gibson, his colleagues at Cornell. In 1995 he chaired the APA task force that wrote a consensus report on intelligence, amid the controversy over the book The Bell Curve.

A documented anecdote

The day after the Challenger disaster in 1986, Neisser and Nicole Harsch asked students to write down where they were when they heard the news. Almost three years later they asked them again. Many gave very different accounts with complete confidence, and some even believed that their own handwriting on the original sheet was wrong.

Criticism, limits and reception

Some laboratory psychologists replied that studies of everyday life lose experimental control and do not allow clear conclusions. Today both approaches coexist. His work on "vivid" memories of public events showed that the confidence with which we remember does not guarantee accuracy, an idea with important consequences in the courts.

References

  1. Neisser, U. (1967). Cognitive Psychology. Nueva York: Appleton-Century-Crofts.
  2. Neisser, U. (1976). Cognition and Reality. San Francisco: W. H. Freeman.
  3. Neisser, U. y Harsch, N. (1992). Phantom flashbulbs: False recollections of hearing the news about Challenger. En E. Winograd y U. Neisser (eds.), Affect and Accuracy in Recall (pp. 9–31). Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
  4. Neisser, U. et al. (1996). Intelligence: Knowns and unknowns. American Psychologist, 51(2), 77–101.
